summary: Specifies Mobile IP for IPv4, which lets a mobile node keep its home address while moving between networks. A home agent forwards traffic to the node's current location. It replaces RFC 3220 and was itself replaced by RFC 5944.

eli5.summary: When you move house, the post office forwards your mail to the new place. Mobile IP does that for a device that moves between networks, so connections do not break.

subtitle: How a device can move between IPv4 networks and keep its address, using a home agent that forwards its traffic.

tldr.problem: IPv4 assumes an address identifies where a node is attached, so a node that moves must either change its address and break its connections, or have host-specific routes spread across the Internet, which does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: The mobile node keeps its home address and registers a care-of address with a home agent on its home network. The home agent intercepts datagrams for the home address and tunnels them to the care-of address.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3344 obsoleted RFC 3220 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 5944, so it is no longer the current Mobile IPv4 specification.

today: RFC 3344 is obsoleted by RFC 5944 and was updated by RFC 4636 and RFC 4721. It was a Proposed Standard that obsoleted RFC 3220, so RFC 5944 is the place to look for the current Mobile IPv4 specification.

sections.title: The Mobility Problem
sections.content:
IPv4 assumes that a node's IP address identifies its point of attachment to the Internet. To change attachment point without losing the ability to communicate, a node has two options: change its address every time (which makes it impossible to keep transport and higher-layer connections alive), or have host-specific routes propagated through much of the routing fabric (which has severe scaling problems). Both are often unacceptable.

This RFC defines a scalable mechanism, Mobile IP, that lets a node change its attachment point without changing its IP address. Its requirements are that a mobile node can communicate after moving without changing its address, that it can still talk to nodes with no mobility support (only the new entities need protocol changes), and that every message that tells another node where the mobile node is MUST be authenticated, to guard against remote redirection attacks.

The protocol assumes mobile nodes will generally not change attachment point more than once per second. It targets "macro" mobility between IP subnets. Where movement stays within one subnet, link-layer handoff may be faster and cheaper.
sections.eli5: Normally your address says where you live, so if you move, your mail gets lost. Mobile IP lets you keep the same address while you travel, so your friends never need to learn a new one.

sections.title: Mobile Nodes, Agents and Care-of Addresses
sections.content:
Mobile IP adds three entities. A mobile node is a host or router that changes its point of attachment. A home agent is a router on the mobile node's home network that tunnels datagrams to it when it is away and keeps its current location. A foreign agent is a router on the visited network that provides routing services to the registered mobile node and detunnels datagrams the home agent sent.

The mobile node has a long-term home address. While away, it also has a care-of address, which is the end of the tunnel and reflects its current attachment point. There are two ways to get one:

  • A foreign agent care-of address is an address of the foreign agent, learned from its advertisements. The foreign agent decapsulates the tunneled datagrams. This mode is preferred because many mobile nodes can share one address, which spares the limited IPv4 address space.
  • A co-located care-of address is a local address the mobile node obtains by other means, such as DHCP, and associates with its own interface. The mobile node decapsulates tunneled datagrams itself. It works where no foreign agent exists, but it uses up addresses on the visited network.

In outline: datagrams sent to the home address are intercepted by the home agent, tunneled to the care-of address, and delivered to the mobile node. In the reverse direction, datagrams from the mobile node are generally delivered with standard IP routing, not necessarily via the home agent.
sections.eli5: Your home address is your permanent street address. Your care-of address is like the hotel where you are staying this week. A helper at home sends your mail on to the hotel, and replies can go straight out.

sections.title: Agent Discovery
sections.content:
Agent Discovery is how a mobile node learns whether it is on its home network or a foreign one, and notices when it has moved. Mobile IP extends ICMP Router Discovery (RFC 1256) for this. An Agent Advertisement is an ICMP Router Advertisement carrying a Mobility Agent Advertisement Extension (extension type 16). An Agent Solicitation is a Router Solicitation whose IP TTL MUST be 1. Advertisements also have a TTL of 1.

The extension carries a sequence number, a Registration Lifetime (the longest lifetime the agent will accept in a Registration Request) and flag bits: R (registration required even with a co-located address), B (busy, no new registrations), H (home agent), F (foreign agent), M and G (can receive minimal or GRE encapsulation), and T (reverse tunneling). At least one of F and H MUST be set. If advertisements are sent periodically, the interval SHOULD be no longer than one third of the advertised ICMP Lifetime, so a mobile node can miss three in a row before dropping an agent.

Advertisements and solicitations need no authentication. A mobile node that finds itself back home deregisters with its home agent and then operates without mobility services.
sections.eli5: When you arrive somewhere new, you look for a sign or ask if there is someone who can help. Helpers on each network shout out that they exist, and a new arrival can also call out and ask who is there.

sections.title: Registration Messages
sections.content:
Once away from home, the mobile node registers its care-of address with its home agent so the home agent can create or update a mobility binding. If it uses a foreign agent care-of address, it MUST register through that foreign agent, which relays the request. Otherwise it registers directly with the home agent. A deregistration at home also goes directly.

Registration uses UDP, with destination port 434. A Registration Request (type 1) holds flag bits (S simultaneous bindings, B broadcast datagrams, D decapsulation by the mobile node, M minimal encapsulation, G GRE encapsulation, T reverse tunneling), a Lifetime in seconds, the Home Address, Home Agent, Care-of Address and a 64-bit Identification used to match replies and to defeat replay. A Lifetime of zero means deregistration and 0xffff means infinity.

A Registration Reply (type 3) carries a Code, the granted Lifetime, the home address and agent, and the Identification. Codes 0 and 1 mean accepted, 64 and up are denials by the foreign agent, and 128 and up are denials by the home agent. Neither agent may increase the Lifetime the mobile node asked for.

Every Registration Request and every Reply from the home agent MUST include an authorization-enabling extension, such as the Mobile-Home Authentication Extension (type 32). Mobile-Foreign (33) and Foreign-Home (34) authentication extensions are also defined. Extensions use a Type-Length-Value format, with two newer grouped formats recommended for future ones.
sections.eli5: Registering is like telling the post office, 'send my mail to this new address for this many days'. You show a secret password so nobody else can pretend to be you and steal your mail.

sections.title: Tunneling and Routing
sections.content:
Home agents and foreign agents MUST support IP in IP encapsulation (RFC 2003). Minimal encapsulation (RFC 2004) and GRE are optional alternatives, used at the home agent's discretion when the mobile node asks.

The home agent MUST be able to intercept datagrams addressed to a registered mobile node's home address. On an Ethernet-like link it does this with proxy ARP, answering ARP Requests for the mobile node with its own link-layer address, and with gratuitous ARP broadcast when the node leaves or returns, to update other nodes' ARP caches.

A foreign agent that receives a tunneled datagram for an address not in its visitor list MUST NOT forward it unmodified, because a routing loop is likely, and SHOULD silently discard it. A foreign agent must route datagrams from registered mobile nodes at least by verifying and recomputing the IP header checksum, decrementing TTL and forwarding to a default router. While away from home, mobile nodes MUST NOT broadcast ARP to find another node's MAC address.

The RFC also covers broadcast and multicast datagrams and mobile routers, and recommends reverse tunneling (RFC 3024) where ingress filtering would drop packets with a topologically incorrect source address.
sections.eli5: The helper at home pretends to be you, grabs your mail and puts it in a bigger envelope addressed to your hotel. At the hotel, the outer envelope is torn off and your mail is handed to you.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Registration makes a mobile node's traffic go to its care-of address. If registration were not authenticated, this would be a serious vulnerability, because remote redirection is a well-known problem. ARP is also unauthenticated, and gratuitous ARP brings all of ARP's risks.

Home agents and mobile nodes MUST be able to authenticate. The default algorithm is HMAC-MD5 with a 128-bit key. The authenticator covers the UDP payload, all prior extensions, and the Type, Length and SPI of its own extension. The older 'prefix+suffix' use of MD5 is considered vulnerable. Foreign agents MUST also support HMAC-MD5, with manually distributed keys, but not every message with a foreign agent has to be authenticated, since key distribution is hard without a key management protocol.

Replay protection uses the Identification field. All mobile nodes and home agents MUST implement timestamp-based protection, and MAY also implement nonce-based protection. The 128-bit key must be secret and pseudo-random. For privacy, users should rely on encryption outside the scope of this document.
sections.eli5: If anyone could say 'please send Sam's mail to me', they could steal it. So every change-of-address request carries a secret signature, and each request is stamped so an old one cannot be replayed.

messages.label: Registration Request
messages.note: Begins registration with the prospective foreign agent.

messages.note: Relayed to tell the node the outcome.

fields.name: r
fields.desc: Sent as zero; ignored on reception.

fields.name: x
fields.desc: Sent as zero; ignored on reception.

fields.name: Lifetime
fields.desc: Seconds before expiry; zero deregisters, 0xffff is infinity.

fields.name: Home Address
fields.desc: IP address of the mobile node.

fields.name: Home Agent
fields.desc: IP address of the home agent.

fields.name: Care-of Address
fields.desc: IP address for the end of the tunnel.

fields.name: Identification
fields.desc: Matches replies to requests and protects against replay.
